name: Micropigmentation / scar tattooing

image.caption: Scar Camouflage- hair loss - scalp micropigmentation - hair tattoo

lead: Micropigmentation, also called paramedical tattooing or permanent makeup, places pigment matched to your surrounding skin into a scar so the contrast shrinks and the scar blends in. The colour change is visible once the pigment is placed.

Encyclopedia references list scar covering, vitiligo camouflage, nipple-areola reconstruction after mastectomy and eyebrow restoration among its medical uses. No clinical studies specific to appearance outcomes were identified.

paras: A trained practitioner deposits the pigment in a clinic or studio, often in more than one session, matching colour to the surrounding skin. It is raised in looksmaxxing discussions mainly for pale or discolored scars.
Tattoos are long-lasting. Conditions that impair wound healing, such as diabetes, may affect choices about location and timing.

angle.text: Micropigmentation tattoos skin-matched pigment into pale or discolored scars so they blend with the skin around them, and the change shows as soon as the pigment is placed. It is established in medical use for scar covering and vitiligo, with little formal outcome data.

lead: Micropigmentation, also called permanent makeup or paramedical tattooing, deposits pigment into the skin to reduce the visibility of scars or pigment differences. In looksmaxxing discussions it is raised as a way to blend pale or discolored scars with surrounding skin.

Encyclopedia references list scar covering, vitiligo camouflage, nipple-areola reconstruction after mastectomy and eyebrow restoration among its medical uses [1]. No clinical studies specific to appearance outcomes were identified for this article.
infobox: Scar camouflage, vitiligo, areola reconstruction, eyebrow restoration

paras: Medical or paramedical tattoos can conceal scars or treatment effects, recreate a nipple and areola after mastectomy, and reduce the visibility of vitiligo patches [1]. Tattoos have also been used to restore eyebrows in conditions such as alopecia [1]. The technique places pigment in the skin to match surrounding tone.

A reference source notes that because diabetes can impair wound healing, people with diabetes may need to consider location and timing of a medical tattoo [1]. The source gives little further detail on risks. Pigment match to surrounding skin and aging of the pigment are discussed by practitioners but were not documented in the sources reviewed.
